summary: RIFT can advertise key/value pairs in Key-Value Topology Information Elements. This Standards Track document specifies behavior for the Key Types (Well-Known, Organizationally Unique Identifier, and Experimental) and a method to structure the values. It also defines a Well-Known Key Sub-Type.

eli5.summary: Routers pass notes labeled with a title and a message. This sets the rules on how to write the labels and organize the messages.

questions: routing in fat trees key types
what is a rift kv tie
what is a rift key target
subtitle: How RIFT routers label and structure the free-form key/value data they flood through a fat-tree fabric.

tldr.problem: RIFT lets routers advertise key/value pairs in Key-Value Topology Information Elements, with no limits on content, so independent implementations need a common way to name keys and lay out values.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a 1-byte Key Type, a 3-byte Key Identifier (or a Key Sub-Type plus a 2-byte Key Sub-Identifier), three key types (Experimental, Well-Known, OUI), a Key Target for steering southbound data, and one Well-Known sub-type for testing tie-breaking.
tldr.outcome: Vendors and operators get stable key spaces and a registry with Expert Review, while RIFT itself is told not to depend on KV data for its own computations.

today: RFC 9992 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2026, and the unit metadata shows no obsoleting or updating RFCs. It builds on RFC 9692, the base RIFT specification.

sections.title: Why Key/Value Data in RIFT
sections.content:
The Routing in Fat Trees protocol (RIFT, RFC 9692) can advertise key/value pairs inside Key-Value Topology Information Elements (KV TIEs). The RFC places no restrictions on what that data holds or what it is used for.

The motivating example is overlay protocol state. Leaf nodes could advertise it up to the Top-of-Fabric (ToF) nodes, so an operator can see the critical state of a fabric-wide service from a single ToF node instead of collecting and reconciling it from many leaves.

What the RFC adds is structure: how keys are named, how values are laid out, and a few behaviors that make interoperability simpler.
sections.eli5: Routers sometimes want to pass along extra notes, like a sticky note on a shared fridge. This RFC makes sure everyone writes the notes in the same tidy way.

sections.title: The Key-Value Structure
sections.content:
Every KV TIE starts with a Key Type, a 1-byte value taken from the RIFTCommonKVTypes registry defined in RFC 9692. Next comes a 3-byte Key Identifier that names the specific key and says what the values mean. Then come the variable-length Values.

Valid Key Types run from 1 to 255, and valid Key Identifiers from 1 to 16777215. Zero is illegal in both fields: it MUST NOT be allocated or used, and a KV TIE received with a zero there MUST be discarded and logged at least once. The Key Identifier SHOULD be unique within its Key Type, and the Values SHOULD hold one or more elements.

The RFC does not limit what the values contain, but it RECOMMENDS defining a KV TIE structure with a serialized Thrift model, as RFC 9692 does for the protocol's own packets, for simpler interoperability.
sections.eli5: Each note has a type sticker, a number on the label and then the message. Zero is never a real number on the label, so a note with zero gets thrown away.

sections.title: Key Sub-Types and the Three Key Types
sections.content:
A Key Sub-Type splits the 3-byte identifier into a 1-byte Key Sub-Type (1 to 255) and a 2-byte Key Sub-Identifier (1 to 65535). Zero is illegal in both, with the same discard-and-log rule. The sub-type MUST be used with the Well-Known and Experimental key types and is OPTIONAL for others.

  • Experimental (Key Type 1): MUST support a Key Sub-Type; the Key Sub-Identifier selects the specific key.
  • Well-Known (Key Type 2): MUST support a Key Sub-Type; sub-types come from a new IANA registry.
  • OUI (Key Type 3): vendor-specific, and an implementation MAY support it. The Key Identifier MUST use the implementing organization's reserved OUI space.
sections.eli5: There are three kinds of labels: one for experiments, one for everyone's agreed-upon notes and one where a company uses its own personal code so it never clashes with others.

sections.title: Design Considerations and Tie-Breaking
sections.content:
Because KV data is unrestricted, the RFC warns that it should not carry topology information that RIFT itself uses for distributed computations. That would likely cause race conditions in convergence, oscillations or other suboptimal behavior.

Nodes that do not recognize a KV TIE, for example because of an unknown Key Type, flood it normally as specified in Section 6.3.4 of RFC 9692. Mixed deployments are therefore fine.

When identical keys arrive from several northbound neighbors, only one KV TIE is selected, and the node picks the one with the highest System ID. To avoid surprises, implementations are RECOMMENDED to compute Values independently but consistently, so several ToFs do not advertise the same key with different values. The RFC notes this can still happen under failure, for example if multiple ToFs become split-brained.

Southbound KV TIE flooding SHOULD avoid network-wide flooding where possible. Key Targets are one mechanism for that.
sections.eli5: If two parents send the same note with different words, the child keeps the note from the parent with the biggest ID number. So parents should agree before writing.

sections.title: The Southbound Tie-Break Sub-Type and Key Targets
sections.content:
The RFC reserves Well-Known Key Sub-Type 127 for testing and verifying tie-breaking of the Southbound Keystore. All implementations MUST support it. Its value carries a REQUIRED System ID and a RECOMMENDED node level, and implementations SHOULD use the normative Thrift model given in the RFC.

A Key Target is an OPTIONAL 64-bit value that identifies the group of nodes meant to receive a KV TIE. All zeros means every node, and all ones means all leaf nodes; neither may be used for any other purpose. Any other value MUST be derived with the normative algorithm, shown in Rust, which sets bits in the 64-bit value from the System ID using three fixed random seeds, in the manner of a Bloom filter.

Key Targets apply only to southbound KV TIEs. They MUST NOT appear northbound, where they are ignored and logged at least once. Nodes that do not process Key Targets keep sending KV TIEs to all nodes in that direction, and Key Targets MUST be preserved when a KV TIE is re-originated southbound.

If a node leaves a Key Target group and the new KV TIE no longer includes the previous Key Target, implementations SHOULD flood the newer instance with a very short lifetime to the nodes that belonged to the old group, so stale copies do not linger in the link-state database.
sections.eli5: A Key Target is like a mailing list code on a note. Only the routers whose codes match need to read it, and when someone leaves the list, they are told to throw their old copy away quickly.

sections.title: IANA Registries and Expert Review
sections.content:
IANA created the RIFT Well-Known Key Sub-Types registry, using the Expert Review procedure, and updated the RIFTCommonKVTypes registry with the values from this document. In the sub-type registry, 0 is Illegal, 127 is the Southbound Tie-Break Sub-Type, and 1-126 and 128-255 are unassigned.

Experts reviewing requests for either registry must check three things: that the request properly defines how identifiers are used (for example as a boolean, an explicit value or an auto-derived value), that it supplies normative Thrift models where applicable, and that work originating outside the IETF does not conflict with work already published or being published.
sections.eli5: There is an official list of label numbers. Before a new one is added, an expert checks that it is clearly explained and does not clash with anyone else's.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says it introduces no new security concerns to RIFT or the specifications it references, because KV TIEs are already extensively secured by the RIFT specification itself (RFC 9692).
sections.eli5: The notes already travel in the same locked mailbag as everything else in RIFT, so this RFC adds no new locks to worry about.

fields.name: Key Type
fields.desc: Identifies the Key Type; 0 is illegal.

fields.name: Key Identifier
fields.desc: Identifies the key and the meaning of its values; 0 is illegal.

items.label: Experimental
items.desc: Uses a Key Sub-Type; Key Sub-Identifier selects the key.

items.label: Well-Known
items.desc: Uses a Key Sub-Type from the IANA registry.

items.label: OUI
items.desc: Vendor-specific; Key Identifier uses the organization's OUI space.
